speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) with the increasing number of COVID-19 cases, whether the current measures are effective in ensuring that Singapore is prepared for COVID-19 to be treated as “endemic”; (b) whether the healthcare system has adequate capacity; and (c) whether new measures are required.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: asked the Minister for Health in what circumstances can COVID-19 patients request the Ministry to have their recovery in community care facilities or hospitals after a positive diagnosis, instead of a quarantine at home.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) how are the younger and fully vaccinated COVID-19 patients being triaged for other home recovery criteria, such as having no severe co-morbidities or vulnerable household members; (b) whether such triaging typically occurs within 24 hours of confirmation of polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test results; and (c) in the longer run, what is the target time to pick these patients up for conveyance to a Government facility from the time they are deemed unsuitable for home recovery.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) when will the Ministry decide on using viral vector or other combinations of vaccines for the third COVID-19 vaccine booster jab; (b) how will this decision impact the booster jab programme for seniors; (c) whether the definition of "fully vaccinated" will be changed to differentiate those who have taken the third booster jab; and (d) if so, how will this be reflected in the TraceTogether app.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: asked the Minister for Health in relation to the Vaccine Injury Financial Assistance Programme (VIFAP) (a) whether the findings of the independent VIFAP Clinical Panel can be released to applicants and, if not, whether this can be done; (b) what avenues are available to applicants to appeal against decisions to reject claims made under the VIFAP; and (c) what are some of the most common grounds for rejecting applications.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Thereafter, Senior Minister of State  Janil Puthucheary will answer Question Nos 10 to 20 for oral answer and Question Nos 27 to 30 for written answer.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And both of us will then take supplementary questions together after our respective answers, please?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are committed to our plans to opening up and transit to a COVID-19-resilient nation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Hence, lockdowns like circuit breakers are no longer an option.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Many workers, families, students and businesses are going to suffer for it, and it will affect our ability to earn ourselves a living in the long term.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Although only a small percentage of infected individuals require hospital or ICU care, we also admit many more others for observation, because they are at risk of developing serious illnesses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, when the infection number rises, all these translate to a larger number of hospital patients, which put considerable strain on our hospitals and healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Hence, even as we continue our journey to transit to a COVID-19-resilient nation, we should also have a care for our hospitals and healthcare workers, and "tap on the brakes" to slow down the rate of transmission.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is why we had to implement the measures under the Stabilisation Phase last week.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Unfortunately, in this rapidly changing and evolving situation, we have to stay agile, adapt and respond quickly.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will try to give as early a notice as possible to businesses, but there is a practical limit to that, and we seek your understanding.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On the Home Recovery Programme (HRP), this is an important part of our response, given that the vast majority of infected individuals have mild or no symptoms.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These individuals do not need special medical care and can, therefore, recover safely at home.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Dennis Tan asked if individuals can request to be sent to an isolation facility instead.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have been considering and accommodating such requests, taking into account the medical conditions of the individuals and their family circumstances.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But it is also important to emphasise that individuals and families should make, and have been making, some adjustments to their living arrangements to make HRP safe and possible at home.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Because it is only with a high take-up of HRP, that our hospitals can focus resources on those who may require greater medical attention, including non-COVID-19 patients who need acute hospital care.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This will enable our healthcare professionals to concentrate on those who need acute hospital care.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In response to Mr Xie Yao Quan, in the initial days of HRP, a fair number of patients without serious symptoms did make their way to the Emergency Departments of hospitals.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We did not compile the numbers but it had led to overcrowding of the Departments.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is, therefore, important for us to iron out all the teething issues of HRP, so that there is a strong sense of assurance as patients undergo HRP.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Over the past few days, such incidences have been significantly reduced.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Over the past week, and with the SAF overseeing and operating the programme end-to-end, we have been ironing out the teething issues, resolving service lapses, including those relating to timeliness of notification and conveyancing, and also improving communications with patients and their families.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Every day, over half of infected individuals will be onboarded on HRP and we expect the proportion to continue to rise.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In recent days, for those eligible for HRP, 93% are contacted promptly and smoothly onboarded.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we still have difficulties contacting the remaining minority because there was either no response or contact details are not accurate.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, this is another teething issue that we are ironing out using IT solutions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for those who are illiterate and do not understand the SMS notifications from MOH, we hope family members, neighbours and volunteers can give them a hand.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That is why our partnership with the People's Association (PA) is very important.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Over the weekend, volunteers have been mobilised to reach out to residents who have been served HRP notifications.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As the patients are generally well, we have also kept the involvement of telemedicine providers quite light and have patients call them only when they need medical attention.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In response to Mr Xie Yao Quan, typically, after a person is detected as COVID-19-positive, MOH will contact him within 24 hours, where triaging will be done and a decision made on whether he will be on HRP or needs to be conveyed to a care facility.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In response to Ms Ng Ling Ling, amongst those on HRP, as of 26 September, about 400 are Persons under Quarantine, who subsequently, tested positive for COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ninety-five percent of them are eligible for HRP and have recovered or are recovering well at home.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Five percent needed to be conveyed to a care facility and this was generally done within 24 hours of the request for conveyance.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ms Sylvia Lim also asked about a related issue concerning the procedures of quarantine and Stay-Home Notices (SHN) for travellers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There have been some changes to the SHN procedures, which were announced last week, namely to align SHN duration with the quarantine duration.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As I have explained at the Multi-ministry Task Force (MTF) press conference over the weekend, the healthcare protocols developed over the past months have become complex and confusing to most people.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are undertaking a holistic and comprehensive review to simplify them, so that people understand them and can, therefore, do their part in the fight against COVID-19, and also help others who are in need of assistance and guidance.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is protection against infection of the Delta variant.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Nevertheless, both vaccines remain very effective in protecting against severe illnesses from COVID-19 infections.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for the Sinovac vaccine, the number of people who have been administered with the vaccine in Singapore is low, at less than 2% of our population, and we do not yet have meaningful data to gauge its effectiveness – whether against infection or against severe illnesses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But the Member who asked this question is probably interested to know about the relative effectiveness of the vaccines.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There has been some international data available, including a fairly extensive study done earlier this year – it was pre-Delta – that was done in Chile, which uses a mixture of vaccines.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our neighbouring countries, too, have released some data.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: All these data showed that just like the mRNA vaccines, breakthrough infections are not uncommon amongst individuals vaccinated with the Sinovac vaccine, but the Sinovac vaccine does accord protection against severe illnesses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For those who are not fully vaccinated due to concerns over medical complications or because they experienced severe side effects after their first dose of mRNA vaccine, they may take the Sinovac vaccine at public hospitals.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To Dr Lim Wee Kiak’s question on whether we intend to grant full registration to the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine, this is something we are looking into, once the longer-term follow-up data is fully available to us and HSA has completed its evaluation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To Mr Dennis Tan's question, we are also waiting for data from Pfizer-BioNTech with the view to extend the use of the vaccine to include children aged five to 11.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These are areas we are proactively working on together with the pharmaceutical companies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Three hundred and fifty thousand of them have taken their jabs or booked an appointment.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think, by now, the numbers have gone up.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Two hundred and forty thousand of them have completed their jabs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, we are off to an encouraging start.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To Ms Ng Ling Ling’s question, the Expert Committee has recommended, and MOH has accepted, that individuals eligible for boosters will include those aged 50 and above and all those who are immunocompromised.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Expert Committee continues to review international data to assess the efficacy and safety of booster shots for younger groups, as well as those exposed to high-risk environments, such as healthcare and frontline workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In time, we will also be inviting eligible individuals who have taken the Sinovac or SinoPharm vaccine to take their mRNA booster shots.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, most of them are not due yet.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For policy consistency, the Vaccine Injury Financial Assistance Programme (VIFAP) will only apply to the vaccines used under our National Vaccination Programme.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ms He Ting Ru asked whether VIFAP applicants would have access to the findings by the Panel as well as avenues for appeal if their applications are rejected.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The VIFAP Clinical Panel assesses applications based on two considerations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, whether the patient’s conditions are related to the COVID-19 vaccination.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The reasons for rejected applications are made known to the applicant and unsuccessful applicants may apply for a reassessment if there are new supporting medical information.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: At this stage, individuals' vaccination status, as listed on the TraceTogether app, will not change, regardless of their booster dose status.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are administering the booster in good time and, so, this issue of expiring vaccination status has not arisen yet.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But, in time, this is an issue that we will need to review.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about the possibility of exploring a combination of vaccines to be used for the booster jab.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Expert Committee on COVID-19 vaccination is still studying the heterologous strategy of administering a non-mRNA booster shot that is different from the first two primary series mRNA doses as data emerges.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the meantime, we will administer mRNA vaccines under the booster programme as the best available data utilise these vaccines for boosting with good effect.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ms Jessica Tan asked if our current measures are effective in ensuring that Singapore is prepared for COVID-19 to be treated as "endemic".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our transition journey to living with COVID-19 is unique in this world, in the sense that we did not allow ourselves to go through big waves of transmission last year, which many countries did and suffered tremendous loss of lives.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Today, when we see other countries opening up and living lives almost normally, let us not forget the heavy price that they have paid last year.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We commenced our transition journey only after we have vaccinated the large majority of our population, so that, for the vast majority of infected persons, they now have no or mild symptoms.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary will elaborate on other parts of the plan.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is still a long battle ahead, which we will prevail as one Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It has been a challenging 20 months for all of us, especially our healthcare workers.
